title: Skew-adjoint generators and unitary flows
subtitle: G2 lecture 040000 · expanded companion
adaptation: Individually authored from the spoken lecture and its display-only mathematical appendix. Includes stepwise constructions, explicit hypotheses, worked examples and topic-specific vector figures; all slide prose is independent of audio.

slides.title: What infinitesimal motions preserve length?
slides.lead: A differentiable linear motion preserves every norm exactly when its generator is skew-adjoint.
body: Let x(t) satisfy x′(t)=Kx(t). To see whether the length remains constant, differentiate its squared norm rather than its norm.
The resulting condition concerns K+K*. If this operator is zero, every instantaneous change is perpendicular to the current position in the real inner-product sense.
slides.takeaway: Length preservation is encoded in the adjoint of the generator.
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 040000 · What infinitesimal motions preserve length?

slides.title: Differentiate a squared length
slides.lead: The product rule turns the geometric requirement into an operator identity.
body: For x′=Kx, differentiating ⟨x,x⟩ gives ⟨Kx,x⟩+⟨x,Kx⟩. If K*=−K, the terms cancel for every x, so the derivative is zero.
This calculation does not require the solution to be a rotation in a single plane. It applies to every finite-dimensional real or complex inner-product space.
slides.takeaway: Skew-adjointness makes each trajectory tangent to its sphere of constant norm.

slides.title: The quarter-turn matrix
slides.lead: The real matrix J rotates a vector through ninety degrees when applied once.
body: It sends (x,y) to (−y,x), so Jᵀ=−J and J²=−I. The differential equation x′=Jx tells a vector to move perpendicular to itself at unit angular speed.
Exponentiating yields the usual planar rotation R(t). For a unit starting vector the trajectory lies on the unit circle, and the tangent vector points in the direction Jx.
slides.takeaway: A constant skew generator yields uniform rotation.

slides.title: The operator-valued solution
slides.lead: The same exponential moves every initial vector at once.
body: Set Q(t)=e^{tK}. Its derivative satisfies Q′(t)=KQ(t), and Q(0)=I. Because K* = −K, the adjoint is Q(t)*=e^{−tK}.
Therefore Q(t)*Q(t)=I. In finite dimensions Q(t) is a unitary operator; in the real setting it is orthogonal. The inverse motion runs time backward.
slides.takeaway: Skew-adjoint generators produce a one-parameter unitary group.

slides.title: The converse: recover the generator
slides.lead: Any differentiable one-parameter unitary group has a skew-adjoint derivative at zero.
body: Assume Q(t)*Q(t)=I and Q(0)=I. Differentiate the identity at t=0. The product rule gives K*+K=0, where K=Q′(0).
This demonstrates necessity as well as sufficiency. In finite dimensions, differentiability plus the group law gives Q(t)=e^{tK}.
slides.takeaway: The generator of a differentiable unitary flow must be skew-adjoint.
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 040000 · The converse: recover the generator

slides.title: Different rotation axes need not commute
slides.lead: In three dimensions there is no single scalar angle that describes every composition.
body: A rotation about the vertical axis followed by one about a horizontal axis need not agree with the reverse order. Their infinitesimal generators generally have K₁K₂ ≠ K₂K₁.

Thus the equality e^{tK₁}e^{tK₂}=e^{t(K₁+K₂)} needs a commutation hypothesis. The sum of skew-adjoint generators is skew-adjoint, but its flow is not generally obtained by multiplying the separate flows.
slides.takeaway: Being length-preserving does not make different rotations interchangeable.
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 040000 · Different rotation axes need not commute

slides.title: Complex notation: the self-adjoint generator
slides.lead: A complex skew-adjoint matrix can be written as i times a self-adjoint matrix.
body: If K*=−K, set H=−iK; then H*=H and K=iH. The unitary flow becomes Q(t)=e^{itH}.
In this form a self-adjoint operator determines the frequencies of the flow through its real eigenvalues, while multiplication by i changes growth into phase rotation.
slides.takeaway: Self-adjoint H describes the spectral rates; iH generates unitary motion.
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 040000 · Complex notation: the self-adjoint generator

slides.title: An eigenvector rotates by phase
slides.lead: For a complex eigenvector Hv=λv, its unitary trajectory is especially simple.
body: Powers of H act by λⁿ on v, so the exponential series gives e^{itH}v=e^{itλ}v. The scalar factor has absolute value one.
Every eigenspace therefore undergoes a phase rotation at a rate set by its eigenvalue. Orthogonality of the eigenspaces lets us combine these motions without changing inner products.
slides.takeaway: The spectral theorem decomposes a unitary flow into independent phase motions.
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 040000 · An eigenvector rotates by phase

slides.title: Changing the angular speed
slides.lead: Multiplying the planar generator by a real scalar changes rotation speed, not length preservation.
body: For K=ωJ with J²=−I, the matrix K is still skew-symmetric. Its flow is Q(t)=e^{tωJ}=R(ωt), so ω controls the signed angular rate.
If ω=2, a quarter-turn occurs at t=π/4. If ω is negative, the orientation reverses. In every case Q(t) remains orthogonal and the square of every vector norm remains constant.
slides.mathtex: e^{t\omega J}=\begin{bmatrix}\cos(\omega t)&-\sin(\omega t)\\\sin(\omega t)&\cos(\omega t)\end{bmatrix}
slides.takeaway: The generator’s scale determines angular velocity while skew-adjointness enforces isometry.

slides.title: Test both directions
slides.lead: A useful reconstruction starts with the squared-norm derivative and ends with the generator identity.
body: Derive d||x||²/dt=0 when K*+K=0. Then start instead from Q(t)*Q(t)=I and differentiate at zero to recover K*+K=0.
Finally check that J gives the planar rotation matrix and explain why noncommuting rotation generators cannot simply be added inside one exponential.
slides.takeaway: Skew-adjointness is the exact infinitesimal criterion for differentiable unitary motion.
